entries.title: You Can See Everything
entries.creator: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim
entries.review:
masterclass. genuinely, there is so much to unpack here that i don't even know where to begin.

what fascinates me most is how much the film manages to communicate through its construction, how every decision feels deliberate, and how the language of cinema itself becomes such an important part of the experience. it's not simply about what we're being shown, but how we're being shown it, what we're being led to believe, and what we're perhaps overlooking in the process.

there's an incredible amount of depth here, both thematically and formally. the film constantly invites you to reconsider what you're watching, to sit with certain ideas, and to question your own interpretations. i’m an absolute sucker for when a film trusts its audience enough to leave things unresolved, when it understands that not every idea needs to be explicitly communicated for it to resonate.

and that's what makes this so special to me. there's something almost overwhelming about how much there is to think about, how many different directions you could take a single scene or idea, and how much of the experience continues to unfold in your head long after it's over. there's simply too much here to fully appreciate all at once.

an incredible piece of filmmaking.

thank you nathan fielder, and lance oppenheim.

entries.review:

thank you, joachim trier.

entries.title: (500) Days of Summer
entries.creator: Marc Webb
entries.review:
i watched this on a day where i completely misread a situation and convinced myself something was a much bigger deal than it actually was.

500 days of summer feels like a movie about the stories we tell ourselves. about how easy it is to get trapped inside your own perspective until it becomes impossible to imagine any other version of events.

what stuck with me wasn’t even the romance. it was the feeling that life keeps moving. that the things currently pinning you down won’t always have the same weight. tom spends so much of the movie drowning in memories and expectations, and somehow comes back up realizing there’s still more waiting for him.

for a movie about heartbreak, it left me feeling strangely hopeful.

thank you angelo.

entries.title: Black Swan
entries.creator: Darren Aronofsky
entries.review:
i spent the first half thinking i knew exactly where this movie was going and then somewhere along the way i realized i couldn't trust a single thing i was watching. the line between reality and obsession gets so blurred that by the end it doesn't even matter whats real anymore because you're trapped in nina's head either way.

that final performance was unbelievable. beautiful and horrifying at the same time. its the feeling of it all. the thrill, the anxiety, the horror, the beauty. every scene feels like its one step away from falling apart and somehow it never lets go of you. i couldn’t look away. it was so visceral. i can’t even say she achieved perfection because the movie makes you question if perfection is even something you're supposed to survive.

entries.title: Paris, Texas
entries.creator: Wim Wenders
entries.review:
the cinematography is breathtaking. every frame feels lonely, like the landscape is carrying the same weight as the people inside it. ry cooder’s score quietly follows that feeling the entire way through, never telling you what to feel, just letting the silence hurt.

but that third act is something else entirely. the booth scene between travis and jane is one of the most heartbreaking conversations I’ve ever watched. harry dean stanton’s performance is so restrained that every word feels heavier than the last, and by the time hunter finally falls into jane’s embrace, it feels less like a resolution and more like a wound finally being allowed to breathe. then travis’ message to hunter… fuck.

what hit me the hardest is that the film understands love isn’t always about staying. sometimes it’s about believing the people you love deserve a chance at a life that you don’t think you can give them. whether travis is right or wrong almost doesn’t matter. it’s the fact that he believes it that makes it so devastating.

beautiful, patient, and quietly crushing. a film that says more in its silences than most movies do with an entire screenplay.

thank you, wim wenders.

entries.title: Ikiru
entries.creator: Akira Kurosawa
entries.review:
i genuinely can’t believe this came out in 1952. it feels timeless. the whole concept of spending your entire life just existing, going through the motions, only to find out you have six months left because of terminal cancer is one of the saddest things i’ve seen put to film.

watanabe realizes he spent decades in limbo, never really doing anything that made him feel alive, and in the little time he has left, he ends up finding more purpose than he ever had before. that final swing scene is one of the most beautiful scenes i’ve ever watched. it’s heartbreaking, but at the same time there’s something so peaceful about it.

kurosawa somehow made a movie over 70 years ago that still feels just as relevant today. we’re all so caught up in routines that it’s easy to forget we’re actually supposed to be living, not just existing.

thank you, akira kurosawa.

entries.title: Her
entries.creator: Spike Jonze
entries.review:
i just finished her and i don’t know how to feel, and i mean that in the best way possible.

it’s crazy the lengths people will go to just to feel understood, to feel seen, to find some kind of human connection. this movie made me feel awkward, confused, happy, sad, hopeful. pretty much everything you can feel as a person. the fact that a relationship between a man and an operating system can evoke all of those emotions says so much about loneliness, intimacy, and what it really means to love someone.

more than anything, though, it left me wanting to be more social. to go out there, to stop being so afraid of what might happen, because the risk of getting hurt is worth the chance of finding something genuine. it also served as a reminder that i have so much love to give… to the people i already hold so dearly, and to the ones i’ll eventually meet.

what a beautiful film.

entries.title: sankofa
entries.creator: redveil
entries.review:
sankofa, an album written and produced by redveil, sounds less like a young artist trying to prove himself and more like someone taking inventory of where he comes from. The album’s title, drawn from the Akan concept of returning to the past to move forward, frames the project as an act of retrieval. Memory, family, identity, and inherited pain are revisited not to dwell in them, but to understand how they shape his present. This album does an excellent job in allowing silence, repetition and plainspoken language to carry weight. Rather than presenting confession as spectacle, redveil lets fragments accumulate — whether that be small encounters, brief details, half-spoken truths — until a portrait emerges. Tragically beautiful. That’s how I would describe a common theme that I don’t see people talk about in the discourse of this album. It circles something deeply personal without spelling it out. When you listen to tracks like glimpse of you, save, and buzzerbeater / black christmas, they begin to feel less like separate songs and more like three vantage points on the same relationship. They can be heard side by side as a younger brother trying to understand love, and survive the distance created by an older brother’s mental health struggles. 

.. ‘buzzerbeater / black christmas’ provides the clearest foundation. Early in the song, he situates his childhood identity in admiration: ‘I just wanna be like my big bro’ and ‘My literacy is innate, I watch my brother do it every week.’ He isn’t just symbolic, he’s formative. Creativity, self-expression, and confidence are inherited through observation. Later, the emotional stakes become unmistakeable: ‘this might be the first show my brother see / he don’t even be with us on Christmas.’ Absence here feels fragile, and unresolved. The closing verse reframes everything with clarity. He writes as if addressing his brother directly: ‘A fractured mind was compromised / and it’s been that way since you could count to five.’ The line recognizes illness not as failure but as something that predates choice. When he adds, ‘I see through the characterization of you as a monster,’ he rejects the way society reads mental illness, especially in Black boys, replacing fear with understanding. The admission ‘my n****, I owe you my life’ demonstrates that even in absence and suffering, the brother continues to be a source of identity and survival.

.. ‘glimpse of you’ captures the emotional reality of the present: love constrained by instability. The repeated refrain ‘I still see a glimpse of you’ suggests fragmentation rather than reunion. He does not encounter this person whole. He encounters traces, flashes, echoes. When he writes ‘even though you let me in your place / you’ll kick me out when paranoia hits,’ the relationship is defined by unpredictability. The detail is clinical without being cold, and it recognizes symptoms without stripping away dignity. What makes the encounter so moving for me is his restraint. He prepares himself emotionally, keeping his updates ‘brief and sparse’ and cherishes whatever time is offered. His goal is heartbreaking, yet modest: ‘I can catch a glimpse of you to take home and put up on the center of my shelf.’ He is not trying to restore the past, but is trying to preserve a version of connection that doesn’t reopen any wounds. Calling this person ‘the bark of my roots’ suggests that they remain foundational to his growth, even at a distance. The love is intact, but proximity is what has changed. The spoken outro from his mother reframes the encounter through compassion rather than tragedy. The biblical story of a man tormented and restrained, later found ‘clothed and in his right mind,’ introduces the possibility of healing without guaranteeing it. This maternal voice we hear at the end transforms the song from a personal visit into a family narrative. One shaped by hope, endurance, and faith.

.. ‘save’ reveals why distance is necessary. The chorus states the thesis clearly: ‘I love you dearly, but I gotta save me.’ This isn’t abandonment, it’s survival. The song wrestles with identity and coping mechanisms formed in youth: ‘self-soothing turned to default presentation / I wore it as a badge of honor’ – suggesting that the roles he adopted to cope with instability became mistaken for personality. He recognizes here that survival strategies, especially those formed early, rarely disappear. They just evolve, sometimes into identities that feel fixed even when they are not. What this song does so well is separate love from proximity. He doesn’t deny this connection, but rather affirms it more directly than in the other songs. However, he acknowledges that closeness, in this scenario, comes with a cost.

The past is not something he escapes, nor something he fully returns to. It is something he learns to carry with more clarity. Taken together, these 3 songs map a relationship across time: admiration in the past, fragmentation in the present, and preservation as a form of survival. They are not separate by any means, but overlapping ones, each informing the other. By the end, sankofa leaves us not with answers, but with a deeper awareness of how one’s identity is shaped. Through memory, through absence and through the difficult choices required to move forward.

bravo, redveil. bravo.

entries.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
entries.creator: Bassam Tariq
entries.review:
there's something so special about a film that can make you feel so much while simultaneously giving you an almost endless amount to think about. i walked away from this genuinely in awe of what i had just watched.

what struck me most was how effortlessly everything comes together. the direction is incredibly assured, the cinematography is gorgeous, and there's such a fascinating relationship between what the film chooses to show and what it allows you to discover for yourself. i found myself constantly drawn to the smaller decisions, the framing, the performances, the way certain scenes are allowed to unfold without feeling the need to overexplain themselves. even when the story takes increasingly unexpected turns, there's an underlying sense of control that makes everything feel purposeful.

what i appreciate most is that the film never feels like it's trying to prove how much it has to say. it simply lets its characters exist within all these contradictions, and trusts us to engage with them. there's tenderness in places where you wouldn't expect it, discomfort in others, and an understanding that people are rarely as simple as the beliefs or circumstances that define them.

there's a beauty in a film that manages to be this ambitious yet so deeply human. absolutely incredible.

*baba was trying to fill shoes three times his size.
why did you leave me?.... why? so i could find my way back to you.*
